Unitree Robotics offers two complementary humanoid plat-forms: the compact G1 \[41\] and the full-size H1 \[42\], tar-geting distinct segments of humanoid research and deploy-ment.
The G1 is a compact, manipulation-oriented humanoid

Unitree G1 is designed as an open and accessible humanoid research platform.
Its ROS2-based software architecture ex-poses low-level control interfaces, sensor streams, and devel-opment tools to researchers, facilitating experimentation with reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and custom control algorithms \[55\].
The platform’s openness has led to growing adoption within academia and has accelerated community-driven software development.
As a result, G1 is increasingly used as a benchmark platform for humanoid robotics research.
...

Robotics companies and universities develop research and experimental models to test new capabilities, such as dynamic balancing, obstacle negotiation, and fine motor skills.
They influence future commercial robots but are rarely available for purchase.

- **Common roles:** R&D in mobility, AI decision-making, and human–robot collaboration scenarios.

- unitree_ros
unitree_ros is a ROS simulation package for Unitree robots.
It contains the urdf files of all Unitree robots.
You can obtain information such as the mass inertia moment limit of the Unitree robot through this package.
At the same time, the unitree_controller and unitree_gazebo packages allow you to quickly Build the simulation verification program in the Gazebo simulator.
- unitree_legged_sdk
unitree_legged_sdk is an SDK package used to develop Aliengo, A1, and Go1 robots in real environments.
You can control the movement of a single joint of the robot based on the low-level development interface, or you can control the robot to move at a specific speed based on the high-level development interface.
...

Its functional positioning is similar to the unitree_legged_sdk package.
...
unitree_ros2 is a function package used to develop Go2 and B2 robots in the ros2 environment.

content.text:
Suitable choices depend on the research goal, budget, and how much you need to modify the robot:

| Platform | Best fit | Considerations |
|---|---|---|
| **Unitree G1** | Bipedal locomotion, balance, manipulation, and embodied-AI experiments. It has developer SDKs and simulation resources, though it is not fully open-source.[2][14] | A practical commercial platform when you want a ready-built robot and established software tools. |
| **Berkeley Humanoid Lite** | Low-cost, hands-on work on locomotion, reinforcement learning, teleoperation, and robot design. Hardware, code, and training frameworks are open-source.[11][12] | Better for teams comfortable assembling and maintaining a platform. |
| **NAO** | Human–robot interaction, education, and accessible experiments with a smaller humanoid.[3][6] | Less suited to research requiring adult-scale strength or advanced whole-body manipulation. |
| **Poppy Humanoid** | Mechanical customization, prototyping, and education using a modular open-source platform.[6] | Check whether its capabilities match your performance needs before selecting it. |
| **Unitree H1** | Full-size locomotion and whole-body control research.[2][14] | More capable at full scale, but likely a larger investment and less oriented toward extensive hardware modification than an open design. |

For a general-purpose lab starting with a commercial humanoid, **Unitree G1** is a strong candidate; for maximum hardware transparency and customization, consider **Berkeley Humanoid Lite**. Before buying, verify access to low-level controls and sensor data, ROS or simulation support, safety features, repairability, and the exact capabilities included in the configuration.
